analysis.one_liner: Allows private student loans to be wiped out in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee and got no vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, student loans are almost impossible to erase in bankruptcy: a borrower must prove the debt imposes an 'undue hardship,' a standard courts interpret very strictly. This bill would change that for private (non-government) student loans, letting borrowers discharge them in bankruptcy the same way they can discharge credit card bills or medical debt. Loans from the government or from schools that are mostly federally funded would keep the stricter rule.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers holding private student loans—often from for-profit colleges or taken out by students who had maxed out federal aid—who can face lifelong collections on debts that would otherwise be wiped in bankruptcy.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the special bankruptcy carve-out for private education loans, so they can be discharged without proving 'undue hardship,' restoring the treatment private loans had before 2005 [S2][S3].
Keeps the stricter 'undue hardship' rule for federal loans and loans from schools whose funds are mostly from the government, so the change is limited to private lenders [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private student lenders and debt collectors, who would recover less on loans from borrowers who file for bankruptcy, and lenders argue that risk could be priced into higher interest rates for new borrowers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private student loan lenders and collectors

drawbacks.text: Lenders warn that easier discharge means more risk for them, which could raise interest rates or shrink the supply of private student loans for new borrowers [S3].
The bill does not touch federal student loans, which make up the large majority of outstanding student debt, so most student-loan borrowers get no relief from it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers in genuine distress with private loans, the change is meaningful: it treats private education debt like other consumer debt. The trade-off is that lenders bear more default risk, which they say could mean higher rates at the margin; the bill's narrow scope means the bulk of student-debt problems—federal loans—remain untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, later to a subcommittee, and neither ever held a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced August 3, 2021 with two cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S4][S5].
On November 1, 2022 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, which took no further action before the Congress ended January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders kept the 2005 bankruptcy protection that makes their loans hard to erase; borrowers with private loans got no relief.

for.name: Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and filed it in the House.

for.name: Danny K. Davis and Eric Swalwell
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the bill drew two cosponsors total.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a markup or floor vote for the entire 117th Congress; sent it to a subcommittee in November 2022.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Democrats; with only two cosponsors, the bill never built the cross-party support needed to move in a House whose calendar was controlled by the majority.

industries.note: Since a 2005 change in bankruptcy law, private education loans can only be discharged if the borrower proves 'undue hardship,' which courts rarely accept. This bill removes that shield for private loans, letting borrowers treat them like ordinary consumer debt; lenders and their debt collectors would recover less on defaults.

industries.industry: Student loan debt collectors and loan servicers
industries.note: Collectors earn on pursuing old private education debt; easier discharge in bankruptcy would end many of those collection streams.
